title: Carry a Mini-Whiteboard With You When Circulating
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton suggests teachers carry their own mini-whiteboard and pen while circulating during independent work, and describes two uses. The first is a running record: jotting down interesting wrong answers, tallying error types to see whether a mistake is isolated or class-wide, and noting names of students producing excellent work, freeing up working memory that would otherwise be spent trying to remember it all. The second, which he calls his favourite, is using the board as a shared working surface during one-to-one interactions — asking a student to reproduce their solution on the board (which often surfaces the error through the act of rewriting itself), then editing it together, and finally extending the student's understanding by swapping numbers or variables into the question on the fly.
points: Barton recommends circulating with a personal mini-whiteboard and pen, not just for students, so the teacher can offload observations rather than trying to hold them in memory.
One use is a running log of wrong-answer patterns and standout work, letting the teacher later judge whether an error is an individual issue or a whole-class problem.
His preferred use is as a shared surface for one-to-one help: having the student rewrite their solution on the board often surfaces the mistake by itself, before any correction is made.

He extends the technique into on-the-fly extension questioning — swapping a number for another number, a negative, or a variable in the same question to test understanding beyond the original problem.
quotes: Quickly writing these down on your mini-whiteboard stops you from having to remember them all, thus freeing up your attention to be responsive to your students’ needs

Say you have spotted a student who has made an error. You crouch down next to them to go through their work and offer your support. Sure, you could do this in the students’ book, but perhaps there is no room next to that question, or the student doesn't want your scruffy writing messing up their neat work
For a start, you can ask the student to reproduce the solution on the board. Often the process of rewriting will result in them spotting their error, and then they can correct it in their book.

But if they don’t, you then have a nice, big, editable solution that you can work with together. You can highlight a section to focus attention and the student can then rub working out with their finger and make a correction.
Then - and I love doing this - once the student seems to understand, you can change a number in the question - rubbing it out and replacing it with a new number - and ask the student
The mini-whiteboard helps you carry out an additional check for understanding that can even take the student’s knowledge beyond what was originally being tested.
